list.listitem: Thorough history taking and continuous observation is extremely important; repeat history after the physical if there are no clues. C
Exclude factitious fever and drug-related fever first. C
Infections (extrapulmonary tuberculosis [TB] most common) followed by neoplasms and multisystem disease are the most common causes of fever of unknown origin (FUO). B
In elderly patients, consider temporal arteritis and adult-onset Still's disease (a rare inflammatory condition that may lead to chronic arthritis and other complications). B

background.definition: FUO is fever without a definable source after initial evaluation. See "Diagnostic Criteria" for the formal diagnostic criteria. This chapter focuses on the nonimmunocompromised adult patient.

list.listitem: In a Spanish cohort study of HIV-infected patients, the incidence of FUO decreased to 7.3 episodes per 100 HIV-infected patients after 1997 corresponding with the introduction of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART).
In a Japanese hospital, 153 of 5245 patients had FUO (prevalence of 29.17/1000).
Of 6250 infectious disease consults performed at three community hospitals in Rhode Island from 1984 to 1990, 86 were FUO (13.6/1000).

In a recent prospective observational study in patients undergoing a structured diagnostic protocol for FUO, 49% of patients received a diagnosis in the following categories: infectious (16%), neoplasia (7%); noninfectious inflammatory disorders (22%), and miscellaneous causes (4%) No cause of the fever was identified in 51% of the patients.

Increased use of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) emphasizes the need to list ICI-associated FUO as a separate category. The mechanism by which ICI cause fever was analyzed in a recent publication .
The etiologies of FUO vary based on the setting and geographic location of the study (see ).
In a Spanish HIV-infected cohort, infectious causes of FUO shifted from disseminated Mycobacterium avium intracellulare, followed by TB, to leishmaniasis in patients receiving HAART.

The thermoregulatory center of the hypothalamus is responsible for regulating the body temperature. This region is susceptible to stimulation by endogenous pyrogens such as cytokines released by monocytes and macrophages in response to exogenous pyrogens such as viruses, bacterial endotoxins, immune complexes, and products of tissue injury.

Major endogenous pyrogens are interleukin-1 (IL-1), IL-6, tumor necrosis factor, and interferons. They act by inducing phospholipases that make arachidonic acid available for prostaglandin synthesis. Prostaglandin E2 increases the thermal set point in the hypothalamus through generation of cAMP.

FUO is defined as at least 3 weeks of illness with fever of 38.3°C (101°F) or higher on several occasions and no diagnosis after 3 outpatient visits or 3 days in the hospital or 1 week of "intelligent and invasive" ambulatory investigation.
Take a thorough history at least twice (before and after the physical). A well-taken history can provide potential clues to the etiology of the fever (see ).
identifies the physical examination findings that might be helpful in pointing toward a specific diagnosis.

CBC, differential, platelet count, and peripheral smear: in a retrospective review study from the Mayo Clinic, 8/8 available peripheral blood smears of patients with multiple myeloma that initially presented as FUO had rouleaux formations.

In 1 study (N = 112 in derivation and 100 in validation cohort), having 2 or 3 of the following: CRP >60 mg/L, eosinophils <40/mm, and ferritin <500 microg/L was predictive of infection in patients with FUO (sensitivity 91.4%, specificity 92.3%).

ESR: Elevated ESR was found to contribute to the diagnosis in 104 of 117 (90%) patients with FUO. In the de Kleijn study, testing for the purified protein derivative of tuberculin (PPD) yielded the diagnosis in 2 patients who turned out to have active TB.

To predict the need for bone marrow biopsy to diagnose hematological disease in patients with FUO, a scoring system was proposed. The scoring system consisted of seven factors that significantly predict hematologic disease based on two cohorts with a total of 102 patients: the presence of leukoerythroblastic changes in peripheral blood followed by ferritin>1000 ng/ml, splenomegaly, platelets <100 x 103/μl, increased lactate dehydrogenase, hemoglobin <10g/dL and absolute neutrophil count <2000/μl.

Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs): In a prospective multicenter study involving 73 patients with FUO, the presence of ANAs was helpful in diagnosing systemic lupus erythematous (SLE) in all 4 patients diagnosed with this disease, but it showed false-positive results in 8 patients.

The merit of chemical investigation is merely to direct the physician to the possible location of the disease and rarely leads to diagnosis. Some of these tests are: blood chemistry panel; serum iron, transferrin, and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC); vitamin B12; and kidney and liver function. For example, in the de Kleijn study, 50% of the patients with FUO were found to have nonspecific liver disturbances, but in only 4% were specific liver diseases found to be the cause of FUO.
Urinalysis including microscopic examination revealed proteinuria in 36/117 (33%) of the patients with FUO in which diagnosis was established in the de Kleijn study.

Culture of blood, urine, sputum, and other fluids as appropriate was found to contribute to the diagnosis in 5% of the patients. In 1 study in Nepal, bone marrow bacterial culture was more often positive than blood culture (16% vs. 5%), particularly in cases of salmonella infection and when the patient had already taken antibiotics.

Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) is a novel, nucleic acid-based method for detection of difficult and unknown pathogens. A study on 149 FUO patients had shown that mNGS detected much more species, had higher negative predictive (67.6%) and total conforming (65.1%) rate, shortened significantly the time to diagnosis, hospital days stay and consumption of antibiotics .

Bone marrow biopsy, in a French case series of 130 patients with FUO, contributed to the diagnosis in 31 cases (diagnostic yield, 23.7% ). Three types of diseases were found: hematological malignancies (25 cases), systemic mastocytosis (2 cases), and disseminated granulomatosis (1 case). Thrombocytopenia (OR 4.9; 95% CI, 1.04-9.30) and anemia (OR 3.24; 95% CI, 1.13-9.34) were the most reliable predictors of usefulness of bone marrow biopsy.A recent retrospective study evaluated the utility of bone marrow aspiration and biopsy in patients with HIV/AIDS and FUO. Bone marrow aspirates contributed to the diagnosis in 24 of the 57 cases (42.1%) by revealing inflammatory elements in the BM including lymphohistiocytic infiltrates, granulomas and/or fungal infection.

Positive testing for HIV, cytomegalovirus (CMV), syphilis (VDRL), and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) can reveal potential underlying infection in symptomatic ambulatory patients. In this population, patients with fever had a 0.66% prevalence of HIV infection.
Abnormal protein electrophoresis contributed to diagnosis in 92 of the 117 patients in which a diagnosis was established in a study of 167 patients.
CT of the abdomen established the diagnosis of splenic abscess in 28 of the 37 patients who presented with FUO.
Colonoscopy and small bowel radiography were helpful in establishing the diagnosis in 19 patients with intestinal TB initially presenting as FUO in Egypt.
Needle biopsies are potentially useful since liver biopsy was helpful in finding the diagnosis in 9% of the patients with FUO while bone marrow biopsy aided in 18% of patients.
Lumbar puncture was found to be helpful in 2 of 11 (18%) patients with FUO.
Order a CXR only if there is clinical evidence of a respiratory illness or if FUO is accompanied by leukocytosis.

In a consecutive series of 351 orotracheally intubated patients with fever, sinus X-rays were helpful in identifying sinusitis as either the sole cause of fever or a contributing cause in 105 (30%) critically ill patients.

In a series of 70 patients with FUO, PET scanning was 88% sensitive and 77% specific in helping establish the final diagnosis. A positive PET scan in this study was defined as an abnormal uptake that pointed to the organ or tissue where the cause of fever was ultimately found. However, PET contributed to the establishment of a final diagnosis in 36% of 124 consecutive patients receiving a PET scan. No data on the total number of FUO patients (those with FUO and no PET scanning) were provided in this study. In another retrospective study of 68 patients with FUO, fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan was useful in establishing the diagnosis in 56%. Similarly, a recent study on 68 patients with FUO found fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan to be superior to gallium-67 SPECT/CT (single photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography) in sensitivity (79% vs. 49%) and clinical contribution (72% vs. 55%) in diagnosing FUO. In contrast, s systematic review, meta-analysis and Delphi exercise of four databases containing 18 studies and 905 patients revealed a pooled diagnostic yield of 56% and failed to support the use of fluorine 18 fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT over the conventional CT given the limited quality of the included studies.

American Journal of Roentgenology Expert Panel recently reviewed the use of FGD PET in patients with FUO and concluded that it contributes useful information in localizing the site of FUO, diagnozing and guiding future management.

The European Association of Nuclear Medicine Infection and Inflammation Committee created a working group that performed literature review based on PICOs with FUO/IUO as population and [18F] FDG-PET/CT as intervention analyzing 69 articles published from 2001 till 2023 and concluded that [18F FDG-PET/CT was helpful in diagnosing the underlying condition in 50-60%of the patients overall .
In a study that used historical controls, the diagnostic frequency of systemic vasculitis as a cause of FUO increased by 6% to 26% after MRI was included in the diagnostic protocol.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to evaluation.

cell.label: FUO suspected. Exclude factitious fever, perform complete history and physical examination. Diagnostic clue present?
Stop or replace drug therapy to exclude drug-related fever.

Repeat history and obtain laboratory testing: CBC; ESR; PPD; CRP; ANA; RF; CMP; Fe, transferrin, TIBC test; vitamin B12; urinalysis; CXR; culture of blood, urine, sputum and other sites; HIV, CMV, VDRL, EBV; SPEP; muscle enzymes. Diagnostic clue?
Echocardiography, CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis; consider colonoscopy. Specific diagnosis suggested?
Continued observation and repeated evaluations. Consider empirical therapy with NSAIDs.

feature.caption: Historical Items That May Help Point to a Diagnosis in Patients With FUO.

tr.td: Drug fever (7-10 days after starting therapy)
Babesiosis, histoplasmosis, malaria, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Lyme disease
Previous cancer or treatment for cancer
Ingestion of unpasteurized diary products, raw meat
Headache with blocked nose or discharge
Common after transplantation of a solid organ
Toothache, loose teeth, intermittent febrile episode following eating

feature.caption: Physical Examination Findings That May Help Point to a Specific Diagnosis in the Patient With FUO.

tr.td: Thickened temporal artery in an older patient
Cardiac murmur that changes with position
Occasional salmon-pink truncal rash, achy or swollen joints with hepatomegaly and splenomegaly
Lack of tears or absent papillary constrictor response
